cognate: Ved. nā́man- = Gk ὄνομα (*h₁nómn̥); Ved. √dhā = Gk τίθημι (*dʰeh₁-); both verbs in the middle voice in the anchors (dádhānaḥ / τίθεσθε)
drift_or_renewal: none in the lexemes. The middle voice differs in use: Vedic dádhānaḥ nā́ma means 'taking a name for oneself' (Indra); Greek τίθεσθε ὄνομα means 'give your own child a name'. Active and passive Vedic uses (dadhāti, dhāyi) match the Greek 'give a name' exactly
shared_syntax: verb *dʰeh₁- with direct object *h₁nómn̥. In the support, the name given is the subject complement (RV 10.115.2 agníḥ ... nā́ma dhāyi; Od. 18.5 Ἀρναῖος ... ὄνομ̓ ... θέτο)
context: Both are naming acts in a ritual or solemn frame. RV 6.44.8 has Indra assume a great name by the poets' words. Od. 19.403-406 has Autolycus told to find the name and the parents to set (τίθεσθε) the name he will speak. The pairing is not generic: Greek and Vedic, like many languages, could have used 'call' (καλέω, √hū) or 'give' (δίδωμι, √dā). Both instead use the 'put' verb, as Hittite lāman dai- does (recalled; the local Hittite hit is fragmentary). The collocation recurs in both corpora (more than 15 RV padas, at least 6 Greek loci)

cognate: Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος = Av. vacah- (*wékʷos; slab maps vácāṃsi to the root wekʷ-); Ved. √takṣ = Av. taš- = Gk τέκτων, τεκταίνομαι (*tetḱ-; slab maps takṣam to tḗtḱti and τεχνῶν to tetḱsneh₂)
drift_or_renewal: Greek keeps the root only in derivatives (τέκτων 'craftsman', denominative τεκταίνομαι). Avestan has frozen the collocation as a compound, vacas-tašti- 'strophe' (literally 'word-fashioning')
shared_syntax: verb *tetḱ- 'fashion (like a carpenter)' with object *wékʷos 'word(s)': Ved. vácāṃsi ... takṣam; Gk ἔπος παρατεκτήναιο (Od. 14.131); agent noun with genitive object ἐπέων ... τέκτονες (Pind. P. 3.113); Av. compound vacas-tašti-
context: In all of these, verbal art is described as carpentry. RV 6.32.1 is the poet's first-person statement that he fashioned words with his mouth for Indra. Pindar calls the poets who made Nestor's and Sarpedon's fame 'carpenters of words'. Od. 14.131 uses the same image, with a negative sense, for making up a tale. CAVEAT ON THE ANCHOR: the slab's Greek partner (Philebus 55e) only co-attests the two roots, in τέχνη and in the idiom ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, without the collocation. The phrase-level Greek evidence is all in support

cognate: Ved. nā́bhi- = Gk ὀμφαλός (*h₃nobʰ-); the seating verb in the support is *sed- in both: Ved. ní asādi (√sad) and Gk καθίζων, ἕδρα (*si-sd-, *sed-)
drift_or_renewal: The 'earth' genitive is renewed: Ved. pr̥thivyā́ḥ against Gk γᾶς and χθονός (χθών is cognate with Ved. kṣam-, but not used in the Vedic phrase). The anchor RV 6.47.28 itself is 'navel of Varuṇa', said of the war-chariot, and is not the cosmic phrase
shared_syntax: locative or prepositional phrase 'at the navel (of earth)', marking where a sacred figure is seated: nā́bhā pr̥thivyā́ḥ / nā́bhā ní asādi hótā ~ γᾶς ὀμφαλόν, ὀμφαλὸν μέσον καθίζων
context: In both traditions the navel of the earth is the cult centre where the divine officiant sits and gives voice. In the Vedic texts the Hotar or Agni sits down or dwells at the navel (the fire altar), and the sacrifice is 'the navel of the world'. In Ion 5-6 Phoebus, seated at the 'middle navel' of Delphi, chants to mortals (ὑμνῳδεῖ βροτοῖς). In Eum. 40-41 a suppliant 'holds his seat' (ἕδραν ἔχοντα) at the omphalos. The cognate head noun, the seating verb from the same root, and the cultic setting all agree. CAVEAT: a 'navel of the world' is a cross-cultural image (Semitic, for example), so convergence cannot be ruled out. The anchors are only loosely congruent
phrase: *h₃nobʰ- 'navel (of the earth)' as the seat of the officiant
